# Runtime APIs and external commands

## Scope

Choose between a runtime or platform API and an external command for a required capability. Own the semantic-fit assessment, command-boundary costs, and justification for retaining that interface when code is introduced, reviewed, or migrated into a language runtime.

## When to update

Update when evidence changes the criteria for semantic fit, command-boundary cost, justified retention, or verification of the selected interface.

## Compare interfaces

Start from required inputs, outputs, failures, lifetime, and supported environments. Prefer a runtime API when it supplies the required semantics and removes an unnecessary command boundary. An external system can be reached through more than one interface; requiring that system does not itself require its CLI.

## Account for arguments

Constructed shell text adds parsing and quoting. Pass separate argument values without a shell where the interface permits it; the target utility still interprets its own grammar.
documents.proposed_addition: An argument vector preserves separate values; an array-shaped parameter does not establish that contract. PowerShell Start-Process -ArgumentList joins array entries into one space-separated command-line string; source string delimiters do not reach the child. When supported and suitable, .NET ProcessStartInfo.ArgumentList accepts separate values and performs escaping. Choose between these interfaces using supported runtimes and process requirements, and exercise the real child with spaces and Unicode. Later shells and utilities still interpret their own grammar.

# PowerShell execution policy

## Scope

Explain how PowerShell execution policy controls whether scripts may run and how callers select a policy scope.

## When to update

Update when policy defaults, supported scopes, or platform enforcement changes.

## Responsibility

This owner explains execution-policy selection and enforcement, not native-program launch arguments.
